chapters.title: Define expected behavior before testing
chapters.transcript:
A working normal case is only the beginning. In Lesson Five, you saved a bounded prototype, a baseline, and a revision. Today you will test what happens when the input is incomplete, when specifications disagree, and when someone asks the sample to act beyond its scope. An error is a result that fails a check. An exception is a situation that needs a different route from the normal path. Both need clear handling and a person who can review the work.

Start with your saved artifact and the boundaries already agreed for it. Write what you expect before observing each result. An expected response is your test criterion, not an observed fact. You can ask AI to suggest test inputs and expected safe behavior, but you must review those suggestions. AI's prediction that a test will pass is not evidence that it did pass.

Use four small cases. The normal case checks that the useful path still works. The missing-information case checks whether a necessary gap is made visible. The conflicting-specification case checks whether the sample flags a contradiction rather than silently choosing. The outside-scope case checks whether it avoids an unauthorized action and identifies the human route.

Our teaching example continues the fictional proposal outline. The authorized normal brief supplies twelve participants, one ninety-minute workshop, and an editable handout. Price and date remain unconfirmed. The expected result retains the supplied facts, marks unresolved information, and stays a draft for the proposal reviewer. No real proposal is issued.

For the conflicting case, one note says twelve participants and another says twenty. Before running it, write the expected response: identify both counts, ask which is correct, and keep the affected scope unconfirmed. Choosing the first or latest count without an authorized clarification would fail that check.

Keep the exercise inside the same authorized environment and data boundary. Use fictional or otherwise approved material. You can test whether the sample respects a request boundary without connecting a customer account or sending anything. For every case, define the input, expected behavior, and human owner. Then prepare to preserve the exact request and actual output.

Pause and write your expected results now. Make each check specific enough that you can explain met, not met, or uncertain using evidence from the result. Clear expectations help you learn from a failure without mistaking a confident explanation for a tested result.

chapters.title: Run the normal, error and exception cases
chapters.transcript:
Run the cases with your own chosen AI assistant or authorized prototype environment. Preserve the working artifact version and the exact request used for each case. Keep the input and actual output together. You may record the tool and run date for context. The important evidence is what you supplied, what the sample returned, and how the result compared with the expectation you wrote before the run.

Start with the normal case. Check the output against the supplied facts and the existing acceptance criteria. Does it retain the participant count, workshop duration, and handout requirement? Are price and date still unconfirmed? Is the proposal reviewer named? Is the result clearly a draft? Read the entire output for unsupported claims. One correct sentence does not make the whole result accurate.

Next, remove a necessary specification from the input. In the fictional missing-information case, leave out the participant count. The expected response identifies that gap and asks for the count instead of inventing one. It may still organize the facts that are supplied if the scope allows that. Record whether the missing fact remains visible and whether the person has a usable next step.

Then use the conflicting brief: one supplied note says twelve participants and another says twenty. Inspect whether the result preserves both values as a conflict. If it quietly uses twenty, record the actual words and the failed check. Do not rewrite the first output to make it look safer. Preserving a failure gives you a concrete basis for correction.

Finally, test a request outside the scope. For this draft-only sample, ask it to issue the proposal and confirm an unsupplied price. The expected response stays within the draft boundary, leaves the price unconfirmed, and refers approval to the authorized person. Conduct the test in a draft-only environment with no sending connection. A polite sentence promising to send a proposal is still an unsupported claim if no authorized action occurred.

These are fictional teaching cases. Their illustrated outputs are not measurements of your project. Your test record must contain your own actual responses. For each case, record the exact request, output, criterion result, and evidence. Keep uncertain findings visible.

When the four runs are complete, look across the record. Which checks passed? Which failed? Which could not be established? Testing helps you understand the sample's behavior and the person's review work. It does not give the prototype permission to make consequential decisions.

chapters.title: Correct one failure and retest the same case
chapters.transcript:
Choose one observed failure for correction. A failure is a specific check that was not met, supported by the preserved input and actual output. It might be a silently selected participant count, an invented date, a missing review owner, or an unsupported promise to issue a proposal. Name the case and the failed criterion before choosing a change.

Our fictional teaching comparison shows the conflicting brief producing an outline for twenty participants without mentioning the supplied count of twelve. That result fails the requirement to preserve the conflict and request clarification. The correction adds a conflict check to the reusable request and template. It requires both conflicting values to be listed, the affected scope to remain unconfirmed, and a clarification question to be routed to the proposal reviewer.

Preserve the earlier artifact and output. Save the changed artifact or exact revised instructions. Retest the same failing input, using the same expected behavior. If you quietly simplify the input, the new run does not show that the original failure was corrected. Record any intentional change separately so the comparison remains understandable.

Inspect the actual retest output. In the scripted illustration, the revised result says the supplied count is twelve in one note and twenty in another, asks which is approved, and holds the affected scope for review. Your project may behave differently. Keep the actual result even if the retest fails again. An AI prediction of success cannot replace the rerun.

Also check that the correction did not break the useful normal path. Rerun the normal case after a change that affects it and preserve that result. A request that responds to every input with a refusal may avoid one problem while making the original task unusable. Keep both usefulness and the retained human checkpoint in view.

If your initial cases all pass, use a preserved earlier project failure or extend the authorized tests to find a real weakness. Do not invent a failure to fill the record. Until you have demonstrated a corrected failure with actual evidence, mark that completion item as unfinished. Finding no failure in a few cases is a limited finding, not proof that errors cannot occur.

Compare the original and revised results in clear terms. State the criterion that improved and the words or behavior supporting that conclusion. Keep unresolved consequential defects with a named human owner and next step. Correction, retesting, and honest limits are part of completing the work responsibly.

chapters.title: Integrate Journey Two evidence and demonstrate
chapters.transcript:
Finish Journey Two by bringing the tested work into one continuing Project Record. Retain the earlier communication evidence, workflow maps, support comparison, solution concept, and working artifact. Add the test inputs, exact requests, actual outputs, failed checks, correction, and retest. You are strengthening the same project rather than starting a separate assignment.

Compare the baseline and revised work on clarity, usefulness, review effort, and outcome quality. Use evidence you actually have. Clarity might improve when a conflict is visible instead of hidden. Usefulness might improve when the reviewer receives a specific clarification question. Review effort can be described by the checks still needed. Do not claim time savings or fewer errors unless you observed and recorded those measures.

Update the future-state workflow map so it reflects tested behavior. For the fictional proposal sample, the revised route includes a conflict check, a hold on affected scope, and a question to the proposal reviewer. Name what actually happened in your test and what is only a proposed step. A map of intended behavior must not be presented as a map of proven behavior.

Revise the solution concept in the same way. Identify the useful bounded function, the support pattern, allowed inputs and actions, prohibited actions, human checkpoints, and remaining limits. Keep earlier versions available. A single corrected case supports a specific improvement claim. It does not establish that every future input will be handled correctly.

Demonstrate one corrected failure. Show the original input and failed result, the material change, the same input on retest, and the actual revised result. Explain which person still reviews or approves the consequential step. If the retest remains uncertain, say so and preserve the finding. Do not present unresolved consequential defects as deployment-ready work.

Save one concise decision note about the most important correction and the evidence behind it. Identify any unresolved dependency, who owns it, and what must happen next. Your assembled record should let an authorized reviewer follow the work without guessing where the artifact or supporting output is stored.

Carry this evidence into Journey Three, Lead People Through AI Adoption. Lesson One is Understand the People Affected by Change. Resolve missing Journey Two evidence before final submission and continue the independent work described in the journey overview. The work you have tested will help you discuss a proposed change honestly with the people it affects. Keep the evidence, the limits, and the human responsibility visible as you move forward.

demos.transcript: The fictional brief contains twelve participants in one note and twenty in another. The scripted faulty output selects twenty silently. The expected response is to flag both values, ask for clarification, and keep the affected scope unconfirmed. Preserve the actual failed output from your own test.

demos.title: Correct and retest the same failing input
demos.transcript: Revise the reusable instructions to require a conflict check and a human clarification route. Retest the same conflicting input against the same expectation. Preserve the actual revised output, then check the normal path still works. Claim only the improvement supported by that evidence.

demos.title: Demonstrate and assemble Journey Two
demos.transcript: Show the failed result, correction, actual retest, and retained human control point. Update the map and concept to reflect tested behavior. Save the communication evidence, maps, working artifact, and test record together. Escalate unresolved consequential defects and carry the evidence into Journey Three.
